title: Chapter 23. Of the Publique Ministers of Soveraign Power
paragraphs: In the last chapter I spoke of the similar parts of a commonwealth; in this I shall speak of the organic parts — namely, the public ministers.

A PUBLIC MINISTER is someone who is employed by the sovereign (whether a monarch or an assembly) in some affair, with authority to represent the person of the commonwealth in that employment. Now, every man or assembly holding sovereignty represents two persons — or, as it is more commonly put, has two capacities, one natural and one political. A monarch bears the person not only of the commonwealth but also of a man; a sovereign assembly bears the person not only of the commonwealth but also of the assembly. Those who serve the sovereign in his natural capacity are not public ministers; only those who serve him in the administration of public business are. So neither ushers, nor sergeants, nor any other officers who attend the assembly merely for the convenience of the men assembled — in an aristocracy or a democracy — nor stewards, chamberlains, cofferers, nor any other officers of a monarch's household, are public ministers in a monarchy.

Of public ministers, some are entrusted with a general administration, either of the whole dominion or of part of it. Of the whole: for example, a predecessor king may entrust a protector or regent with the whole administration of the kingdom during an infant king's minority. In that case, every subject is obliged to obey so far as the ordinances the protector makes, and the commands he gives, are issued in the king's name and are not inconsistent with the king's sovereign power. Of a part, or province: as when a monarch or a sovereign assembly gives general charge of it to a governor, lieutenant, prefect, or viceroy. Here too, everyone in that province is obliged to obey whatever the deputy does in the sovereign's name, provided it is not incompatible with the sovereign's right. Such protectors, viceroys, and governors have no right beyond what depends on the sovereign's will, and no commission given to them can be read as a declaration of intent to transfer the sovereignty itself, unless it says so in express and unmistakable words. This kind of public minister resembles the nerves and tendons that move the various limbs of a natural body.

Others have a special administration — that is, charge of some particular business, either at home or abroad. At home, first, for the economy of the commonwealth: those who have authority over the public treasure — tributes, impositions, rents, fines, or any other public revenue — to collect, receive, disburse, or audit it, are public ministers. Ministers, because they serve the representative person and can do nothing against his command, or without his authority; public, because they serve him in his political capacity.

Second, those who have authority over the militia — to hold custody of arms, forts, and ports; to levy, pay, or lead soldiers; or to supply anything needed for war by land or sea — are public ministers. But a soldier without a command, though he fights for the commonwealth, does not for that reason represent its person, because there is no one for him to represent it to. Everyone who holds a command represents the commonwealth only to those he commands.

Those who have authority to teach, or to authorize others to teach, the people their duty to the sovereign power, and to instruct them in what is just and unjust — so as to make them fitter to live in godliness and at peace among themselves, and to resist the public enemy — are also public ministers. Ministers, in that they do this not by their own authority but by another's; public, because they do it (or should do it) by no authority but the sovereign's. The monarch, or the sovereign assembly, alone has direct authority from God to teach and instruct the people; no one but the sovereign receives his power Dei Gratia in the strict sense — that is, by the favor of God alone. Everyone else receives it by the favor and providence of God together with their sovereign's: in a monarchy, Dei Gratia et Regis (by the grace of God and the king), or Dei Providentia et Voluntate Regis (by the providence of God and the will of the king).

Those to whom jurisdiction is given are also public ministers. For in their seats of justice they represent the person of the sovereign, and their sentence is his sentence. As already explained, all judicature is essentially bound up with sovereignty, so all other judges are merely ministers of whoever holds the sovereign power. And since controversies are of two sorts — of fact, and of law — so are judgments: some of fact, some of law. Consequently, in the same controversy there may be two judges, one of fact, the other of law.

In both these kinds of controversy, a further dispute may arise between the party being judged and the judge himself. Since both are subjects of the sovereign, this dispute ought in fairness to be judged by men both parties agree on, for no man can be judge in his own case. But the sovereign is already agreed on as judge by both, and so may either hear the case and decide it himself, or appoint as judges whomever they both agree on. This agreement is understood to come about in various ways. First, if the defendant is allowed to challenge any of his judges whose interest makes him suspect — since the complainant has already chosen his own judge — then the judges he does not challenge are ones he has himself agreed to. Second, if he appeals to some other judge, he can appeal no further, since his appeal was his own choice. Third, if he appeals to the sovereign himself, and the sovereign gives sentence — either in person or through delegates the parties agree on — that sentence is final, for the defendant is then judged by his own judges, that is, by himself.

Considering these features of just and rational judicature, I cannot help remarking on the excellent design of the courts of justice established in England for both Common Pleas and Public Pleas. By Common Pleas I mean those where both the complainant and the defendant are subjects; by Public Pleas (also called Pleas of the Crown) I mean those where the complainant is the sovereign. There were two orders of men, one the lords and the other the commons. The lords had the privilege that in all capital crimes their judges could be none but lords — as many of them as chose to attend — and since this was always acknowledged as a privilege granted to them, their judges were none but those they themselves wanted. In every controversy, every subject (and likewise the lords, in civil controversies) had as judges men from the county where the matter in dispute lay, against whom he could raise objections, until at last twelve men were agreed on without objection, and he was judged by those twelve. So, having judges of his own choosing, the party could allege nothing against the sentence being final. These public persons — with authority from the sovereign power either to instruct or to judge the people — are members of the commonwealth that may fitly be compared to the organs of voice in a natural body.

Public ministers also include all those who have authority from the sovereign to procure the execution of judgments given, to publish the sovereign's commands, to suppress uprisings, to apprehend and imprison wrongdoers, and to perform other acts that help preserve the peace. Every act they perform under this authority is the act of the commonwealth, and their service corresponds to that of the hands in a natural body.

Public ministers abroad are those who represent the person of their own sovereign to foreign states. These are ambassadors, messengers, agents, and heralds, sent by public authority and on public business.

But those sent by the authority only of some private faction within a troubled state, though they are received, are neither public nor private ministers of the commonwealth, because none of their actions have the commonwealth as their author. Likewise, an ambassador sent by a prince to offer congratulations or condolences, or to attend a ceremony, is a private person — though his authority is public, the business is private and belongs to the prince in his natural capacity. Also, if a man is sent secretly into another country to explore its counsels and strength, then although both the authority and the business are public, since there is no one there to acknowledge any person in him but his own, he is only a private minister — yet still a minister of the commonwealth, and may be compared to an eye in the natural body. And those appointed to receive the people's petitions or other information, serving as it were as the public ear, are public ministers, and represent their sovereign in that office.

Neither a counsellor nor a council of state — considered simply as having no authority of judicature or command, but only of giving advice to the sovereign when it is asked for, or offering it when it is not — is a public person. For the advice is addressed to the sovereign alone, and his person cannot, in his own presence, be represented to him by anyone else. But a body of counsellors is never without some further authority, either of judicature or of direct administration. In a monarchy, they represent the monarch when delivering his commands to the public ministers. In a democracy, the council or senate presents the outcome of its deliberations to the people as a council; but when it appoints judges, hears cases, or gives audience to ambassadors, it acts in the capacity of a minister of the people. And in an aristocracy, the council of state is the sovereign assembly itself, and gives counsel to no one but itself.
